en.greeting: Hi! Today we travel around the English-speaking world: the words and sounds of six varieties, and how to be clearly understood when English is the language you share. One honest note first: our audio is one voice, so in the recordings, listen for the words.

steps.title: Many Englishes, all valid
steps.text: In B2 you saw that UK, US and Australian English differ in tendencies: the r in *car*, the soft d in *water*, the Australian *day*. Now we widen the map.
steps.body: English has many **varieties**: British, American, Australian, and also **Indian**, **Singaporean** and **Nigerian** English, used every day at work, in universities and in government. Each has its own words, sounds and rhythm, and **all are equally valid**. Your Indonesian English is a variety too. **Honest note:** our audio is **one voice with one accent**, so the recordings in this lesson practise the **words** of each variety. For the real accents, watch the video in the resources.

pairs.id: ragam (bahasa Inggris suatu negara atau daerah)
bahasa bersama antar-orang yang bahasa ibunya berbeda

steps.title: Words that tell you the variety
steps.text: Accents can be hard, but words are easier: learn the common local ones.
steps.body: If you hear a word you don't know, it may be a **local word**, not your mistake: ask *Sorry, what does … mean?* Trap: in the UK the **first floor** is one level **above** the ground floor, but in Indonesia *lantai 1* is the street level. And Indian **revert** means *reply*, not *go back*. In Singapore, **Singlish** is the informal version; at work you'll mostly hear Standard Singapore English.

pairs.id: lantai 2 (satu lantai di atas ground floor)

steps.title: Listen: a message from Melbourne
steps.text: Jess, a colleague in Australia, leaves Rina a voice message. Listen for a typically Australian word.

question.listen: Hi Rina, it's Jess from the Melbourne office. No worries about the report being late. Just send it to me this arvo, and we can go through it together tomorrow morning.
question.prompt: Listen to Jess. When should Rina send the report?
options: This afternoon
Tomorrow morning
This evening
question.explanation: In Australian English **arvo** = afternoon, so *this arvo* = this afternoon. *Tomorrow morning* is when they will go through the report together, not when Rina sends it. **No worries** = it's fine.

steps.title: Listen: a message from Bengaluru
steps.text: Priya, a colleague in India, leaves Budi a voice message. Listen for two Indian English words.

question.listen: Hello Budi, it's Priya from the Bengaluru office. Small change: the client call has been preponed from Thursday to Tuesday, same time. Please revert by tonight if your team can't join.
question.prompt: Listen to Priya. What does she ask Budi to do by tonight?
options: Go back to the old time for the call
Reply if his team can't join the call
Send the slides to the client
question.explanation: In Indian English **revert** = reply, so *Please revert by tonight* = please answer by tonight. It doesn't mean *go back*: the call is **preponed**, moved earlier, to Tuesday. Slides aren't mentioned.

steps.title: The r after a vowel
steps.text: Recap from B2: Americans say the r in *car*; most English and Australian speakers don't. Now the full map.
steps.body: The **r after a vowel** (*car*, *card*, *four*) is one of the clearest clues. **Usually said:** the US and Canada, Ireland, Scotland, much of India. **Usually not said** when no vowel follows: most of England, Australia, Singapore, Nigeria. These are tendencies. Non-r speakers still say the r in *red* and *very*, and before a vowel: *far away* → 'faa-raway'. Indonesians always say the r, and that's fine too.

pairs.id: jauh sekali · r tetap dibaca sebelum vokal: 'faa-raway'
air · US (ulangan B2): t seperti d lembut, 'wader'

steps.title: Which statement is true?
steps.text: No audio: use the map of the r.

question.prompt: Which statement about the r in words like 'car' and 'card' is true?
options: Only American English pronounces this r; every other variety drops it.
Speakers in the US, Scotland and much of India usually pronounce it; most speakers in England, Australia and Singapore usually don't.
Speakers in England don't pronounce any r at all, not even in 'red' or 'very'.
question.explanation: The r after a vowel is usually said in the US and Canada, Scotland, Ireland and much of India, and usually not in most of England, Australia, Singapore and Nigeria. It's not only American. And speakers who drop it still say the r before a vowel, as in *red* and *very*.

steps.title: Rhythm and other sounds
steps.text: Next clue: the rhythm, and a few typical sounds.
steps.body: UK, US and Australian English are **stress-timed**: stressed syllables (suku kata yang ditekan) keep a beat and weak ones shrink to 'uh'. Indian, Singaporean and Nigerian English are often **syllable-timed**, like Indonesian: similar length, clearer vowels. Also often: **India**: t and d with the tongue tip curled back; one sound between v and w. **Singapore**: the last consonant soft or dropped. **Nigeria**: full vowels in weak syllables. In all three: *think* → 'tink'. Different, not wrong.

pairs.id: berirama tekanan: suku kata lemah dipendekkan (UK, US, Australia)
berirama suku kata: tiap suku kata kira-kira sama panjang (India, Singapura, Nigeria, Indonesia)
India: t dan d dengan ujung lidah melengkung ke belakang (retroflex)
India: v dan w sering satu bunyi, di antara keduanya
Singapura: p di akhir sangat lemah, 'bas-sto'

steps.title: A call with Mumbai
steps.text: No audio: use what you know about Indian English.

question.prompt: On a call, Arjun from your Mumbai office says something that sounds like 'wery' for 'very' and 'vest' for 'west'. What's the best explanation?
options: He doesn't know the words 'very' and 'west'.
He's using Singlish particles.
Many Indian English speakers use one sound, between v and w, for both letters; the context tells you the word.
question.explanation: Many Indian English speakers have one sound, somewhere between v and w, for both letters. It's a feature of the variety, not a gap in his vocabulary, so use the context: *the west wing*, *very good*. Singlish particles (lah, leh, lor) are Singaporean and are words, not sounds.

steps.title: English as a lingua franca
steps.text: Many of your English conversations will be with other non-native speakers: Japanese, Thai, German, Korean partners. That's English as a **lingua franca** (ELF).
steps.body: In ELF, **clear beats clever**. Avoid idioms, slang and abbreviations (*touch base*, *ASAP*, *EOD*). Say key numbers digit by digit and type them in the chat; spell names; write dates as *3 April*. Check with a summary, not *Do you understand?*: Indonesians, like many people, say *yes* to be polite (sungkan). Research on ELF (the **Lingua Franca Core**) shows that clear consonants, long vs short vowels and stress on the key word matter much more than a native accent.

pairs.en: Let me put it another way.
Could you spell that for me?
Could you type it in the chat?
Sorry, could you say that more slowly?

steps.title: Listen: a supplier in Osaka
steps.text: You're on a video call with a crackly line. Listen to Kenji, then choose the best reply.

question.listen: Hello, this is Kenji Watanabe from Osaka. Please send the signed contract to my assistant, Ms Tsuchiya, before the thirteenth. She will check it and send it on to our lawyers.
question.prompt: Listen to Kenji. Which reply is best in this lingua franca call?
options: Just to confirm: before the thirteenth, one-three. Could you spell your assistant's name for me?
No worries, I'll get the ball rolling and send it ASAP!
Yes, yes, OK.
question.explanation: It checks the key number (*one-three*, so thirteen isn't confused with thirty) and asks him to spell a name that is easy to get wrong. *Get the ball rolling* is an idiom and *ASAP* an abbreviation: unclear for many partners. *Yes, yes, OK* checks nothing.

id.greeting: Hai! Hari ini kita berkeliling dunia berbahasa Inggris: kata dan bunyi dari enam ragam, dan cara berbicara supaya jelas dimengerti saat bahasa Inggris menjadi bahasa bersama. Satu catatan jujur dulu: audio kita hanya satu suara, jadi di rekaman, dengarkan kata-katanya.

steps.title: Banyak ragam bahasa Inggris, semuanya sah
steps.text: Di B2 kamu melihat bahwa bahasa Inggris UK, US dan Australia berbeda dalam kecenderungan: r di *car*, d lembut di *water*, *day* versi Australia. Sekarang petanya kita perluas.
steps.body: Bahasa Inggris punya banyak **ragam** (variety): Inggris, Amerika, Australia, dan juga bahasa Inggris **India**, **Singapura** dan **Nigeria**, yang dipakai setiap hari di kantor, kampus dan pemerintahan. Tiap ragam punya kata, bunyi dan iramanya sendiri, dan **semuanya sama sahnya**. Bahasa Inggris orang Indonesia juga sebuah ragam. **Catatan jujur:** audio kita **satu suara dengan satu aksen**, jadi rekaman di pelajaran ini melatih **kata-kata** khas tiap ragam. Untuk aksen yang asli, tonton video di bagian sumber.

pairs.id: ragam (bahasa Inggris suatu negara atau daerah)
bahasa bersama antar-orang yang bahasa ibunya berbeda

steps.title: Kata-kata yang menandai ragamnya
steps.text: Aksen bisa sulit, tapi kata-kata lebih mudah: pelajari kata lokal yang umum.
steps.body: Kalau kamu mendengar kata yang tidak kamu kenal, mungkin itu **kata lokal**, bukan kesalahanmu: tanyakan *Sorry, what does … mean?* Jebakan: di Inggris, **first floor** adalah satu lantai **di atas** lantai dasar, padahal di Indonesia *lantai 1* adalah lantai di permukaan jalan. Lalu **revert** versi India berarti *membalas*, bukan *kembali*. Di Singapura, **Singlish** adalah versi santainya; di kantor kamu lebih sering mendengar Standard Singapore English.

pairs.id: lantai 2 (satu lantai di atas ground floor)

steps.title: Dengarkan: pesan dari Melbourne
steps.text: Jess, rekan kerja di Australia, meninggalkan pesan suara untuk Rina. Dengarkan satu kata yang khas Australia.

question.listen: Hi Rina, it's Jess from the Melbourne office. No worries about the report being late. Just send it to me this arvo, and we can go through it together tomorrow morning.
question.prompt: Dengarkan Jess. Kapan Rina harus mengirim laporannya?
options: This afternoon
Tomorrow morning
This evening
question.explanation: Dalam bahasa Inggris Australia **arvo** = afternoon (siang/sore), jadi *this arvo* = sore ini. *Tomorrow morning* adalah waktu mereka membahas laporannya bersama, bukan waktu Rina mengirimnya. **No worries** = tidak apa-apa.

steps.title: Dengarkan: pesan dari Bengaluru
steps.text: Priya, rekan kerja di India, meninggalkan pesan suara untuk Budi. Dengarkan dua kata khas bahasa Inggris India.

question.listen: Hello Budi, it's Priya from the Bengaluru office. Small change: the client call has been preponed from Thursday to Tuesday, same time. Please revert by tonight if your team can't join.
question.prompt: Dengarkan Priya. Apa yang ia minta Budi lakukan paling lambat malam ini?
options: Go back to the old time for the call
Reply if his team can't join the call
Send the slides to the client
question.explanation: Dalam bahasa Inggris India **revert** = membalas, jadi *Please revert by tonight* = mohon dibalas paling lambat malam ini. Artinya bukan *kembali*: call-nya **preponed**, dimajukan, ke hari Selasa. Slide tidak disebut sama sekali.

steps.title: r setelah vokal
steps.text: Ulangan dari B2: orang Amerika membaca r di *car*; kebanyakan orang Inggris dan Australia tidak. Sekarang peta lengkapnya.
steps.body: **r setelah vokal** (*car*, *card*, *four*) adalah salah satu petunjuk paling jelas. **Biasanya dibaca:** Amerika dan Kanada, Irlandia, Skotlandia, sebagian besar India. **Biasanya tidak dibaca** kalau tidak ada vokal sesudahnya: sebagian besar Inggris, Australia, Singapura, Nigeria. Ini kecenderungan. Penutur tanpa r tetap membaca r di *red* dan *very*, dan sebelum vokal: *far away* → 'faa-raway'. Orang Indonesia selalu membaca r, dan itu juga tidak apa-apa.

pairs.id: jauh sekali · r tetap dibaca sebelum vokal: 'faa-raway'
air · US (ulangan B2): t seperti d lembut, 'wader'

steps.title: Pernyataan mana yang benar?
steps.text: Tanpa audio: pakai peta bunyi r tadi.

question.prompt: Pernyataan mana tentang r di kata seperti 'car' dan 'card' yang benar?
options: Only American English pronounces this r; every other variety drops it.
Speakers in the US, Scotland and much of India usually pronounce it; most speakers in England, Australia and Singapore usually don't.
Speakers in England don't pronounce any r at all, not even in 'red' or 'very'.
question.explanation: r setelah vokal biasanya dibaca di Amerika dan Kanada, Skotlandia, Irlandia dan sebagian besar India, dan biasanya tidak dibaca di sebagian besar Inggris, Australia, Singapura dan Nigeria. Jadi bukan hanya Amerika. Dan penutur yang tidak membacanya tetap membaca r sebelum vokal, seperti di *red* dan *very*.

steps.title: Irama dan bunyi lainnya
steps.text: Petunjuk berikutnya: iramanya, dan beberapa bunyi yang khas.
steps.body: Bahasa Inggris UK, US dan Australia **berirama tekanan** (stress-timed): suku kata yang ditekan menjadi ketukan, suku kata lemah menyusut jadi 'eu'. Bahasa Inggris India, Singapura dan Nigeria sering **berirama suku kata** (syllable-timed), seperti bahasa Indonesia: panjangnya mirip, vokalnya lebih jelas. Sering juga: **India**: t dan d dengan ujung lidah melengkung ke belakang; satu bunyi di antara v dan w. **Singapura**: konsonan terakhir lemah atau hilang. **Nigeria**: vokal penuh di suku kata lemah. Di ketiganya: *think* → 'tink'. Berbeda, bukan salah.

pairs.id: berirama tekanan: suku kata lemah dipendekkan (UK, US, Australia)
berirama suku kata: tiap suku kata kira-kira sama panjang (India, Singapura, Nigeria, Indonesia)
India: t dan d dengan ujung lidah melengkung ke belakang (retroflex)
India: v dan w sering satu bunyi, di antara keduanya
Singapura: p di akhir sangat lemah, 'bas-sto'

steps.title: Telepon dengan Mumbai
steps.text: Tanpa audio: pakai pengetahuanmu tentang bahasa Inggris India.

question.prompt: Dalam telepon, Arjun dari kantor Mumbai mengucapkan sesuatu yang terdengar seperti 'wery' untuk 'very' dan 'vest' untuk 'west'. Apa penjelasan yang paling tepat?
options: He doesn't know the words 'very' and 'west'.
He's using Singlish particles.
Many Indian English speakers use one sound, between v and w, for both letters; the context tells you the word.
question.explanation: Banyak penutur bahasa Inggris India punya satu bunyi, di antara v dan w, untuk kedua huruf itu. Itu ciri ragamnya, bukan karena ia tidak tahu katanya, jadi pakai konteksnya: *the west wing*, *very good*. Partikel Singlish (lah, leh, lor) itu khas Singapura, dan berupa kata, bukan bunyi.

steps.title: Bahasa Inggris sebagai lingua franca
steps.text: Banyak percakapan bahasa Inggrismu akan terjadi dengan sesama penutur non-native: mitra dari Jepang, Thailand, Jerman, Korea. Itulah bahasa Inggris sebagai **lingua franca** (ELF).
steps.body: Dalam ELF, **jelas lebih penting daripada keren**. Hindari idiom, slang dan singkatan (*touch base*, *ASAP*, *EOD*). Ucapkan angka penting digit per digit dan ketik di chat; eja nama; tulis tanggal seperti *3 April*. Cek dengan ringkasan, bukan *Do you understand?*: orang Indonesia, seperti banyak orang lain, bilang *yes* karena sungkan. Penelitian tentang ELF (**Lingua Franca Core**) menunjukkan bahwa konsonan yang jelas, vokal panjang vs pendek dan tekanan pada kata kunci jauh lebih penting daripada aksen penutur asli.

pairs.en: Let me put it another way.
Could you spell that for me?
Could you type it in the chat?
Sorry, could you say that more slowly?

steps.title: Dengarkan: pemasok di Osaka
steps.text: Kamu sedang video call dengan sambungan yang putus-putus. Dengarkan Kenji, lalu pilih jawaban terbaik.

question.listen: Hello, this is Kenji Watanabe from Osaka. Please send the signed contract to my assistant, Ms Tsuchiya, before the thirteenth. She will check it and send it on to our lawyers.
question.prompt: Dengarkan Kenji. Jawaban mana yang paling tepat dalam percakapan lingua franca ini?
options: Just to confirm: before the thirteenth, one-three. Could you spell your assistant's name for me?
No worries, I'll get the ball rolling and send it ASAP!
Yes, yes, OK.
question.explanation: Jawaban ini mengecek angka penting (*one-three*, supaya thirteen tidak tertukar dengan thirty) dan meminta ia mengeja nama yang mudah salah. *Get the ball rolling* adalah idiom dan *ASAP* singkatan: tidak jelas bagi banyak mitra. *Yes, yes, OK* tidak mengecek apa pun.
